design_detail: Cochrane systematic review with meta-analyses (CD011612.pub3, published 12 September 2021; an update of Caddy et al., 2015, from a protocol published in 2015; amended 13 September and 17 November 2021 for typographical errors) of double- or single-blind randomized trials of ketamine, esketamine and 14 other glutamate receptor modulators against placebo, active comparators or ECT in adults with unipolar major depressive disorder (trials with fewer than 20% of participants with bipolar depression were allowed). CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, two trial registers and five regulators' websites searched without language or publication-status limits to 30 July 2020; 64 studies (5299 participants), of which 54 contributed data. Risk of bias with the 2011 Cochrane tool, certainty with GRADE; random-effects Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios and inverse-variance (standardised) mean differences; response and remission counted against all randomized participants (dropouts as non-responders); crossover trials contributed first-period data only; outcomes at 24 hours (primary), 72 hours, 1, 2 and 4 weeks and 3 months. This card concerns mainly ketamine against placebo (14 trials with data), ketamine against midazolam (5) and esketamine against placebo (9).
can_establish: What the randomized evidence up to July 2020 shows, with GRADE certainty, about response, remission, depression scores, suicidal ideation, dropout and specific adverse events after ketamine or esketamine compared with placebo or midazolam in adults with unipolar depression, at fixed times from 24 hours to 3 months after treatment began.
cannot_establish: Effects beyond the short term (the trials were short and few reported 3-month data), relapse or maintenance (not studied), long-term or rare harms such as bladder or cognitive damage (adverse events were mostly reported on the day of treatment), effects under conditions where blinding held (most trials did not test it, and it failed in all but one of the five ketamine trials that did), or whether racemic ketamine and esketamine differ (one head-to-head trial of 63 people).

sample.recruitment: Update searches by the Cochrane Common Mental Disorders information specialist on 30 July 2020 (CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase and PsycINFO from 2015; earlier years through the group's register to 9 January 2015), the WHO ICTRP and ClinicalTrials.gov, the websites of the FDA, MHRA, EMA, PMDA and TGA, reference lists of included studies, reviews and textbooks, and correspondence with trialists and experts; no restriction on language or publication status. 6909 records, 3096 duplicates removed, 3603 excluded on title and abstract, 210 full texts retrieved, 39 new studies (Methods › Search methods; Results › Results of the search).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Double- or single-blind RCTs (published or unpublished) in people aged 18 or over with a primary diagnosis of unipolar major depressive disorder by standard operational criteria; studies with less than 20% bipolar participants allowed; treatment-resistant samples allowed; quasi-randomized trials, trials not describing allocation as randomized, diagnosis by screening cut-off or ICD-9, serious medical illness and postpartum depression excluded; monotherapy or add-on, any dose, route, frequency and duration (Methods › Criteria for considering studies for this review).
sample.demographics: Women 0% to 87.5% of participants by study; mean age 25.7 to 58.7 years, with two studies restricted to older adults (above 60); 24 outpatient, 20 inpatient, 5 mixed and 15 unclear settings; 23 trials in the USA, 16 in Asia, 8 in Europe, 3 in Australia, 1 each in New Zealand and South America, 9 cross-continental and 3 unclear; 31 single-centre (Results › Included studies › Setting; Participants). Five studies included bipolar participants (5.56% to 25%) and one included psychotic depression in 10 of 32 participants.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Response and remission were computed against all randomized participants with dropouts counted as non-responders; five trials were rated at high risk for incomplete outcome data, among them Fedgchin 2019 (higher withdrawal in the esketamine arms) (Methods › Measures of treatment effect; Results › Incomplete outcome data).
sample.selection_effects: Most trials were small (50 of 64 had fewer than 100 participants) and most participants had treatment-resistant or severe depression. The ketamine-placebo comparison mixes single intravenous infusions, courses of infusions, one oral trial and three trials in which ketamine was given with the anaesthetic for a course of ECT (Anderson 2017, Chen 2017, Loo 2012); the esketamine-placebo comparison mixes seven intranasal add-on trials, all rated at high risk of other bias for industry funding or the authors' industry employment or payments (three stated to be funded by Janssen), with one intravenous trial and one trial in which esketamine was given with ECT anaesthesia (Jarventausta 2013). Ten included studies could not contribute data (Discussion › Potential biases in the review process).

exposure.measurement: Drug as given in each trial (intended dose, route, schedule, co-interventions and sponsorship extracted; Methods › Data extraction and management).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported in the review: ketamine against placebo was intravenous in 13 of 14 trials (nine at 0.5 mg/kg, three randomizing 0.2 or 0.5 mg/kg, one at 0.3 mg/kg) and oral in one (50 mg a day for six weeks, given as 25 mg twice daily with sertraline); eight trials gave a single infusion, two gave infusions twice weekly, two three times weekly and one randomized to two or three a week; three gave ketamine at each ECT session. Ketamine against midazolam: single intravenous doses from 0.1 to 1.0 mg/kg against midazolam, six infusions over 12 days, or intranasal racemic ketamine 100 mg (one pilot of five people). Esketamine against placebo: intranasal 28 to 84 mg twice weekly for four weeks in most trials (one week in Daly 2018), intravenous 0.20 or 0.40 mg/kg (Singh 2016 b), and 0.4 mg/kg before propofol for ECT (Jarventausta 2013). These are trial conditions, not recommendations (Results › 1. Ketamine versus placebo, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Characteristics of included studies).
exposure.polysubstance: Concomitant psychiatric medication was allowed in most trials: in 10 of the 14 ketamine-placebo trials existing medication continued, four required a drug-free period, three combined ketamine with ECT, and in Hu 2016 and Arabzadeh 2018 ketamine or placebo was added to a newly started antidepressant (escitalopram, sertraline); the intranasal esketamine trials added esketamine or placebo spray to a newly initiated or optimised oral antidepressant in both arms (Results › 1. Ketamine versus placebo, 4th paragraph; Characteristics of included studies › Hu 2016, Arabzadeh 2018, Fedgchin 2019, Popova 2019, Fu 2020, Ionescu 2020, Ochs-Ross 2020). The authors list the unclear role of concomitant medication as a research question (Implications for research).

comparison.controls: Placebo (saline infusion, matched capsules, or intranasal spray with a bittering agent), midazolam as an active placebo (0.02 to 0.045 mg/kg intravenously in four of the five trials with data; 4.5 mg intranasally in the five-person pilot Gálvez 2018), other active agents (thiopental or methohexital or propofol as ECT anaesthetics, remifentanil), ECT, and esketamine in one head-to-head trial (Methods › Comparator interventions; Characteristics of included studies).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: response, a reduction of at least 50% from baseline on the HRSD, MADRS or another depression scale, or CGI-I of 1 or 2 (the review's definition replaced trial definitions); and adverse events (any, and 18 named events, with all reported events collected and grouped post hoc). Secondary: remission (HRSD-17 below 7, longer HRSD versions below 8, MADRS below 11, QIDS-SR16 below 6, or CGI-S of 1 or 2); depression scale scores (MD or SMD of change scores); suicidality; cognition; quality of life; costs; dropouts for any reason, for lack of efficacy and for adverse effects (Methods › Types of outcome measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard depression scales; the continuous outcome was MADRS or HRSD in every included study. Response and remission were imputed from continuous data for 10 studies with a validated method (Furukawa 2005), and missing SDs for one (Results › Included studies › Outcomes).
outcomes.operationalization: Fixed time windows after the start of treatment: 24 hours (12 to 36 hours; the primary time point), 72 hours (37 to under 96 hours), 1 week (4 to 10 days), 2 weeks (11 days to under 3 weeks), 4 weeks (3 to 6 weeks), 3 months (7 weeks to 6 months) (Methods › Timing of outcome assessment). In single-dose trials these are times after one dose; in course trials they fall during treatment, so a 4-week estimate in a four-week esketamine course is an end-of-course effect, not persistence after treatment ended. All participants were people with depression; there are no healthy-volunteer data.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The 9 counts the outcome families the authors say they prespecified (Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence); each was analysed at up to six time points in 22 comparisons, with subgroup and sensitivity re-analyses, and adverse events as up to about 50 separate event types in one comparison, each tested at p < 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Two authors independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts; two extracted data with disagreements resolved by a third (the abstract says three authors independently identified studies, assessed quality and extracted data); five authors assessed risk of bias independently (Methods › Data collection and analysis).

analysis.effect_sizes: Random-effects pooled estimates (fixed-effect for most single-study adverse events), with 95% CIs, I-squared and GRADE. Ketamine against placebo: response at 24 hours OR 3.94 (1.54 to 10.10), 7 studies, 185 participants, I2 14%, absolute 8.8% against 27.4%, very low certainty; at 72 hours 15.84 (3.68 to 68.12), 4 studies, 83; at 1 week 3.76 (0.98 to 14.42), 5 studies, 196; at 2 weeks 2.92 (0.48 to 17.78), I2 83%; at 4 weeks 1.37 (0.50 to 3.77); at 3 months 1.95 (0.24 to 15.69). Remission at 24 hours 5.60 (1.07 to 29.46), 3 studies, 75, absolute 2.4% against 12.0%, very low certainty; 72 hours 6.60 (1.51 to 28.92); 1 week 4.64 (1.37 to 15.68); 2 weeks 1.67 (0.38 to 7.27); 4 weeks 1.46 (0.54 to 3.95); 3 months 1.09 (0.45 to 2.67). Depression scores SMD at 24 hours -0.87 (-1.26 to -0.48), 8 studies, 231, very low certainty; 72 hours -0.68 (-1.28 to -0.07); 1 week -0.72 (-1.10 to -0.33); 2 weeks -0.43 (-0.90 to 0.04); 4 weeks -0.68 (-1.07 to -0.29), 2 studies, 107. All-cause dropout OR 1.25 (0.19 to 8.28), 6 studies, 201, I2 75%, very low certainty. Ketamine against midazolam: response at 24 hours OR 2.48 (1.00 to 6.18), 4 studies, 296, absolute 25.9% against 46.5%, very low certainty; remission 2.21 (0.67 to 7.32), 2 studies, 122, low certainty; SMD -0.49 (-0.87 to -0.10), 4 studies, 297, very low certainty; dropout 0.33 (0.05 to 2.09), 1 study, 72, low certainty. Esketamine against placebo: response at 24 hours OR 2.11 (1.20 to 3.68), 5 studies, 1071, I2 50%, absolute 15.0% against 27.1%, low certainty; remission 2.74 (1.71 to 4.40), 5 studies, 894, absolute 7.2% against 17.5%, moderate certainty; SMD -0.31 (-0.45 to -0.17), 4 studies, 824, moderate certainty; at 4 weeks response 1.84 (1.44 to 2.37), remission 1.57 (1.18 to 2.10), SMD -0.27 (-0.39 to -0.16); all-cause dropout 1.58 (0.92 to 2.73), 5 studies, 773, moderate certainty. Numbers needed to treat, promised in the methods for significant results, are not reported.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable (no meta-regression). Prespecified subgroups by setting (inpatient, outpatient) and age, and sensitivity analyses excluding bipolar or psychotic participants, treatment-resistant samples and trials with dropout above 20%, plus post hoc exclusions of multiple-dose trials and of trials with add-on ECT, were run for ketamine and esketamine against placebo (Data and analyses › Comparisons 23 to 35).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol (Issue 4, 2015) and first review (Caddy 2015). Declared differences: ECT added as a comparator, any validated quality-of-life measure accepted, the adverse-effects objective removed (only RCT data used), the severity threshold changed from 27 to 25 on the HRSD-17, and more detail on the random-effects model (Differences between protocol and review). Not declared: the planned sensitivity analyses excluding trials with unclear allocation concealment or unclear blinding, trials with unfair dose comparisons, and trials with imputed response or borrowed SDs are not reported anywhere in the review; the companion adverse-events search was run but not used; numbers needed to treat were planned but not given.
analysis.selective_reporting: Adverse events are described in the text only where statistically significant; dropouts due to adverse effects were not reported for any summary-of-findings comparison. Forest plots and the risk-of-bias figures are images. Ten included studies contributed no data.
analysis.power: The authors state that most included trials were small (50 of 64 under 100 participants), that most comparisons contain one study and that the largest single analysis has eight studies; imprecision is a reason for downgrading in most summary-of-findings rows.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In adults with unipolar depression, mostly treatment-resistant, ketamine (mostly a single intravenous infusion) was associated with more response and remission and lower depression scores than placebo from 24 hours to one week, at very low certainty, with no clear difference at 2 weeks, 4 weeks or 3 months in response or remission. A 4-week difference in depression scores (SMD -0.68) rests on two trials that combined ketamine with a newly started antidepressant (editors' inference from the participant counts, see key findings). Against midazolam the 24-hour differences were smaller (response OR 2.48, lower limit 1.00; remission interval 0.67 to 7.32). Esketamine, given in four-week courses added to an oral antidepressant in most trials, was associated with more response and remission and lower scores than placebo at 24 hours and at the end of four weeks (SMD about -0.3; low to moderate certainty), with large increases in dissociative symptoms, dizziness, vertigo, nausea and blood-pressure changes. No trial showed a difference in suicidal ideation, and blinding failed in every trial that tested it except one with concurrent ECT.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract is mostly hedged in line with GRADE, but it says that against midazolam ketamine "increases remission rates at 24 hours" although the interval runs from 0.67 to 7.32, and it reports a single odds ratio (3.94) for response and remission together. The conclusions say continued esketamine showed no effectiveness at 72 hours or one week, whereas the results show significant score differences at both times and a significant response difference at one week. The plain language summary says ketamine's effects clearly disappeared after two weeks, while the pooled 4-week score difference is significant (in two add-on trials). The Discussion reads null results from two small trials as suggesting that ketamine is not an effective treatment for suicidality, and the implications say neither drug prevents relapse at three months, which no included trial tested. The Discussion and implications give certainty ranges (very low to moderate; very low to high) that do not match the summary-of-findings tables (all very low for ketamine against placebo; at most moderate for esketamine).

timeline.event: Berman et al., the first randomized crossover trial of ketamine in depression (described in the review's background as seven patients; included here with 9 enrolled and 7 in the first period).
Caddy et al., first version of this Cochrane review (25 studies, 1242 participants), and McCloud et al., its companion review in bipolar depression.
Turner, 'seven concerns' critique of esketamine's efficacy evidence and FDA approval (Lancet Psychiatry), cited in this review and written by one of its authors.
Correia-Melo et al., the only head-to-head trial of racemic ketamine and esketamine in the review (63 participants, intravenous infusions, no difference in response to one week).
This update (64 studies, searches to July 2020).
Nikolin et al., meta-regression of 49 RCTs to April 2023 (read in this batch as sc_nikolin_2023), which shares most of the ketamine and esketamine trials pooled here.

replication.where_it_stands: The Cochrane review remains the most conservative synthesis of the short-term trials: first-period crossover data only, response counted against all randomized participants, and GRADE certainty of very low (ketamine against placebo) to moderate (esketamine against placebo). Later syntheses such as Nikolin et al. (2023) draw largely on the same trials, so agreement between them is not independent replication.

what_would_settle_it: As the authors say: long-term randomized non-inferiority trials comparing repeated ketamine with esketamine and with other active treatments, with an active control that mimics ketamine's acute effects, measured and reported blinding, follow-up of months after the course, systematic adverse-event recording (including bladder and cognitive outcomes), and monitoring of use in routine practice.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, interventions, comparators, outcomes and time points specified.

Published Cochrane protocol (2015) with a differences section that justifies four changes; three planned sensitivity analyses (by allocation concealment or blinding, unfair dose comparison, imputation) and the planned numbers needed to treat are missing without explanation.
Randomized trials only, double- or single-blind, first-period crossover data, with the reason given (to rely on the most robust data and avoid carry-over).
Four databases, two trial registers, five regulators, reference lists, contact with trialists and experts, no language or publication-status limits, search 13 months before publication.
Two authors independently at title, abstract and full-text stages, with a third for disagreements.
Two authors extracted with a piloted form, disagreements by consensus or a third author, data entry double-checked.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The text reports 174 excluded studies (main reasons design 44, secondary publication 26, wrong population 24), but the excluded-studies table and reference list give 18, with reasons that do not match those counts; one of the 18 (Shiroma 2020) is also an included study.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Each characteristics table gives diagnosis, N, age, sex, baseline severity, interventions with doses and schedules, concomitant treatment and outcomes; setting, country and follow-up duration are not given per study.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: 2011 Cochrane tool, all domains, by five authors independently, with supporting quotations; blinding was judged on the procedures described, and high where trials reported failed blinding. Several 'low' allocation-concealment judgments are supported by quotations about sequence generation or blinding (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Sponsorship was extracted, but funding appears in the tables only where it led to a high 'other bias' rating (14 industry-funded trials) or occasionally otherwise; it is not reported for each study.

Random-effects Mantel-Haenszel and inverse-variance methods with fixed-effect checks, first-period crossover data, intention-to-treat counting and validated imputations. The pooling of ECT-adjunct trials with standalone ketamine trials is a clinical-heterogeneity concern, addressed only by a post hoc sensitivity analysis.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: The planned sensitivity analysis excluding trials with unclear allocation concealment or blinding was not reported; risk of bias enters only through GRADE downgrading.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Certainty downgraded for blinding of outcome assessment; failed blinding is called a major limitation likely to bias the effect estimate, and the plain language summary says it may have inflated the effects.
I-squared reported throughout; prespecified subgroup and sensitivity analyses run and discussed; conclusions withheld where heterogeneity was high (ketamine at 2 weeks, 4 weeks and 3 months).

No funnel plot or test (too few studies per analysis); the only discussion is that unpublished trials may remain unknown, and no summary-of-findings row is downgraded for it, although registers and regulators were searched.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Sources of support and declarations given; two listed authors have no declaration printed and no management of the declared interests is described.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence when more than one critical item fails: here item 7 (the excluded-studies list covers 18 of the 174 exclusions reported) and item 15 (publication bias neither tested nor its likely impact discussed). Both are reporting and feasibility problems rather than weaknesses of the core methods: the review is protocol-based, searched comprehensively including regulators, worked in duplicate, used only first-period crossover data, counted response against all randomized participants and graded certainty for its main comparisons. A reader who accepted the shorter excluded-studies list would rate it low confidence. In practice the review can be cited for its pooled short-term estimates with their GRADE ratings, for the time course (24 hours to 3 months), for adverse events relative to placebo and midazolam, and for the failure of blinding in the trials that tested it; it cannot be cited for long-term efficacy, relapse prevention, rare harms or a difference between racemic ketamine and esketamine.

key_findings.finding: 64 studies with 5299 participants were included (31 ketamine, 9 esketamine, 5 memantine, 4 lanicemine and 1 or 2 each of 12 other agents); 48 were placebo-controlled, 48 had two arms, 19 recruited only treatment-resistant participants (inadequate response to at least two antidepressants); most ketamine trials gave a single intravenous dose, while all esketamine trials used repeated doses, most often twice a week for four weeks and mostly intranasally. 54 of the 64 studies contributed data to meta-analyses.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Main results, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Discussion › Potential biases in the review process, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ketamine against placebo, response at 24 hours: OR 3.94 (95% CI 1.54 to 10.10; 7 studies, 185 participants; I2 14%), assumed 8.8% without and 27.4% with ketamine (18.7 more per 100, 4.1 to 40.4 more), very low certainty (downgraded for imprecision and, by two levels, for unclear or high risk in blinding of outcome assessment). At 72 hours OR 15.84 (3.68 to 68.12; 4 studies, 83); at 1 week 3.76 (0.98 to 14.42; P = 0.05; 5 studies, 196); at 2 weeks 2.92 (0.48 to 17.78; I2 83%); at 4 weeks 1.37 (0.50 to 3.77; I2 59%); at 3 months 1.95 (0.24 to 15.69; 3 studies; I2 80%).
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 1, response row and footnotes 1 and 2; Results › A. Ketamine versus placebo › 1.1 Efficacy: number of participants who respond to treatment

key_findings.finding: Ketamine against placebo, remission: at 24 hours OR 5.60 (1.07 to 29.46; 3 studies, 75; I2 0%), assumed 2.4% against 12.0% (9.6 more per 100, 0.2 to 39.4 more), very low certainty; at 72 hours 6.60 (1.51 to 28.92; 4 studies, 83); at 1 week 4.64 (1.37 to 15.68; 5 studies, 196); no difference at 2 weeks (1.67, 0.38 to 7.27), 4 weeks (1.46, 0.54 to 3.95) or 3 months (1.09, 0.45 to 2.67; 2 studies, 90).
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 1, remission row; Results › 1.3 Efficacy: number of participants who achieve remission

key_findings.finding: Ketamine against placebo, depression scale scores: SMD at 24 hours -0.87 (-1.26 to -0.48; 8 studies, 231; I2 41%), very low certainty; 72 hours -0.68 (-1.28 to -0.07; 6 studies, 148); 1 week -0.72 (-1.10 to -0.33; 6 studies, 143); 2 weeks -0.43 (-0.90 to 0.04; 5 studies, 236; I2 65%); 4 weeks -0.68 (-1.07 to -0.29; 2 studies, 107).
key_findings.locator: Results › 1.4 Change scores on depression scale from baseline; Data and analyses › Comparison 1, outcome 1.27
key_findings.note: Editors' inference from the participant counts: the two 4-week studies (107 participants) are outpatient trials (Comparison 23.3, 2 studies, 107), one of them multiple-dose with 81 participants and one single-dose with 26 (Comparisons 29.3.5 and 31.3.5), which fits Arabzadeh 2018 (daily oral ketamine added to newly started sertraline, 81 completers) and Hu 2016 (one infusion added to newly started escitalopram, 27 completers). The review does not name them; the forest plot is an image.

key_findings.finding: Ketamine against placebo, other outcomes: suicidal ideation did not differ at any time (for example MD 0.02, -0.78 to 0.82, at 24 hours, 1 study, 48; 0.34, -0.25 to 0.93, at 72 hours, 2 studies, 68); all-cause dropout OR 1.25 (0.19 to 8.28; 6 studies, 201; I2 75%), assumed 34.0% against 39.1%, very low certainty; quality of life (EQ-5D-3L index at 2 weeks) MD 0.11 (-0.05 to 0.27; 1 study, 64); cognition favoured ketamine in one study of 127 (immediate memory MD 0.80, short-term memory 6.90, long-term memory 4.50).
key_findings.locator: Results › 1.5 Suicidality; 1.6 Cognition; 1.7 Quality of life; 1.9 Acceptability: total dropouts; Summary of findings 1; Data and analyses › Comparison 1, outcomes 1.29 and 1.30
key_findings.note: The only cognition study with 127 completers is Chen 2017, in which ketamine 0.3 mg/kg was added to propofol anaesthesia for a course of 12 ECT sessions (Wechsler Memory Scale-Chinese Revision); it says nothing about ketamine given as an antidepressant on its own.

key_findings.finding: Ketamine against placebo, adverse events more frequent with ketamine: agitation or anxiety OR 3.44 (1.07 to 11.04; 3 studies, 143), confusion 3.76 (1.13 to 12.47; 2 studies, 76), dissociative symptoms 7.72 (1.31 to 45.51; 3 studies, 145); no difference in about 20 other event types, including hallucinations 2.19 (0.45 to 10.78) and nausea or vomiting 1.83 (0.81 to 4.13).
key_findings.locator: Results › 1.2 Adverse events; Data and analyses › Comparison 1, outcomes 1.3, 1.6, 1.7, 1.11, 1.17

key_findings.finding: Ketamine against midazolam (5 studies): response at 24 hours OR 2.48 (1.00 to 6.18; 4 studies, 296; I2 58%), assumed 25.9% against 46.5%, very low certainty; at 1 week 3.11 (1.38 to 7.04; 2 studies, 126); remission at 24 hours 2.21 (0.67 to 7.32; 2 studies, 122), low certainty, with no significant difference at any time; SMD at 24 hours -0.49 (-0.87 to -0.10; 4 studies, 297), very low certainty, and -0.57 (-1.10 to -0.04) at 4 weeks in 1 study of 86; suicidal ideation MD -1.32 (-2.52 to -0.12; 1 study, 57); dropout OR 0.33 (0.05 to 2.09; 1 study, 72), low certainty.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 2; Results › B. Ketamine versus other pharmacologically active agents › 2. Ketamine versus midazolam › 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, 2.9
key_findings.note: The suicidal-ideation analysis of 57 participants matches the secondary publication of Murrough 2013 (Price 2014; Characteristics of included studies › Murrough 2013, Notes).

key_findings.finding: Ketamine against midazolam, adverse events on the day of infusion: blurred vision OR 8.52 (1.80 to 40.39; 1 study, 72), dizziness 3.42 (1.44 to 8.14; 2 studies, 224) and nausea or vomiting 3.62 (1.13 to 11.58; 2 studies, 152) more frequent with ketamine; general malaise OR 0.18 (0.04 to 0.75) and sleepiness or drowsiness OR 0.21 (0.07 to 0.66) less frequent with ketamine; increased blood pressure or heart rate at 1 week OR 9.37 (2.49 to 35.25; 1 study, 54); none of these differences persisted at one week or later, except as stated.
key_findings.note: The text says sleepiness was more likely with ketamine, but the odds ratio (below 1) and the parallel general-malaise sentence indicate the opposite; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Esketamine against placebo (9 trials): response at 24 hours OR 2.11 (1.20 to 3.68; 5 studies, 1071; I2 50%), assumed 15.0% against 27.1%, low certainty; at 1 week 1.60 (1.09 to 2.34; 6 studies, 1115); at 2 weeks 1.57 (1.09 to 2.28); at 4 weeks 1.84 (1.44 to 2.37; 5 studies, 1117); not at 72 hours (1.34, 0.92 to 1.96). Remission at 24 hours 2.74 (1.71 to 4.40; 5 studies, 894), assumed 7.2% against 17.5%, moderate certainty; at 2 weeks 1.52 (1.07 to 2.16); at 4 weeks 1.57 (1.18 to 2.10); not at 72 hours (1.55, 0.91 to 2.64) or 1 week (1.54, 0.88 to 2.69).
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 3; Results › D. Other glutamate receptor modulators versus placebo › 9. Esketamine versus placebo › 9.1 and 9.3

key_findings.finding: Esketamine against placebo, depression scale scores: SMD at 24 hours -0.31 (-0.45 to -0.17; 4 studies, 824), moderate certainty; 72 hours -0.30 (-0.50 to -0.11; 3 studies, 517); 1 week -0.23 (-0.37 to -0.10; 884 participants); 2 weeks -0.21 (-0.34 to -0.07; 4 studies, 857); 4 weeks -0.27 (-0.39 to -0.16; 6 studies, 1182); no difference at 3 months (-0.12, -0.75 to 0.52; 1 study, 38). Suicidal ideation did not differ at any time (for example MD -0.15, -0.44 to 0.15, at 24 hours; 2 studies, 450). All-cause dropout OR 1.58 (0.92 to 2.73; 5 studies, 773; I2 8%), assumed 8.5% against 12.9%, moderate certainty.
key_findings.locator: Results › 9.4 Change scores on depression scale from baseline; 9.5 Suicidality; 9.9 Acceptability: total dropouts; Summary of findings 3

key_findings.finding: Esketamine against placebo, adverse events more frequent with esketamine: dissociative symptoms OR 8.76 (5.19 to 14.77; 4 studies, 933), vertigo 12.25 (4.09 to 36.67; 3 studies, 796), sensory disturbance 7.25 (3.55 to 14.78), feeling drunk 7.58 (1.37 to 41.77; 2 studies, 571), sedation 5.31 (2.18 to 12.94), postural dizziness 4.70 (1.06 to 20.80), constipation 4.07 (1.60 to 10.39), dizziness 3.67 (2.54 to 5.31), paresthesia or neuropathy exacerbation 3.51 (1.62 to 7.62), nausea or vomiting 3.24 (1.84 to 5.72), blurred vision 3.02 (1.37 to 6.66), change in blood pressure 2.67 (1.52 to 4.70; 4 studies, 933) and sleepiness or drowsiness 2.11 (1.39 to 3.21).

Head-to-head and other comparators: racemic ketamine against esketamine (Correia-Melo 2020, 63 participants, intravenous infusions over 40 minutes of ketamine 0.5 mg/kg or esketamine 0.25 mg/kg) showed no difference in response at 24 hours (OR 1.07, 0.40 to 2.89), 72 hours (1.56, 0.58 to 4.22) or 1 week (2.34, 0.85 to 6.45); against ECT (Ghasemi 2013, 18 participants, single-blind) response favoured ketamine at 24 hours (OR 28.00, 2.07 to 379.25) and 72 hours (12.25, 1.33 to 113.06) but not later; comparisons with ECT anaesthetics and remifentanil rest on one or two small trials.
key_findings.locator: Results › 7. Ketamine versus esketamine › 7.1; C. Ketamine versus ECT › 8.1; 3. Ketamine versus thiopental to 6. Ketamine versus remifentanil hydrochloride

key_findings.finding: Blinding: risk of bias for blinding was judged on the procedures described, not on blinding achieved. Of the 31 ketamine trials, five tested blinding and it failed in all but one (Anderson 2017, ketamine given with ECT anaesthesia). Examples from the characteristics tables: in Fava 2018, clinicians guessed the 0.5 mg/kg ketamine assignment correctly in 100% and participants in 77%; in Sumner 2020, 88% identified their ketamine session; in Tiger 2020, every participant given ketamine was convinced of it. 22 of 64 studies were at low risk for blinding of participants and personnel, 4 high and 38 unclear.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies, 2nd paragraph; Blinding › Blinding of participants and personnel; Characteristics of included studies › Fava 2018, Sumner 2020, Tiger 2020 (risk-of-bias tables)

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses: excluding the three ECT add-on trials left the ketamine-placebo response at 24 hours unchanged (OR 3.94, 7 studies, 185) but changed later estimates, for example response at 1 week from 3.76 (5 studies, 196) to 14.32 (2.90 to 70.64; 3 studies, 75) and at 2 weeks from 2.92 (I2 83%) to 15.73 (4.71 to 52.51; 2 studies, 85). Excluding multiple-dose trials, the 4-week score difference was -0.43 (-1.21 to 0.35; 1 study, 26). Esketamine estimates were unchanged by the sensitivity analyses.
key_findings.locator: Data and analyses › Comparisons 1, 31 and 32 (summary tables); Discussion › Summary of main results › Efficacy: Ketamine versus placebo, 3rd paragraph; Efficacy: esketamine, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that the review supports a short-term antidepressant effect of ketamine against placebo and midazolam, and of esketamine against placebo, that there was no evidence of a longer-term effect of acute ketamine after one week, and that confidence is limited by performance bias and the small number of trials per comparison (most comparisons have one study; the largest single analysis has eight).
key_findings.locator: Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Other glutamate receptor modulators: very little evidence; isolated single-trial differences for citicoline (remission at 4 weeks, OR 3.27, 1.01 to 10.62), decoglurant (response at 4 weeks, 2.04, 1.23 to 3.38) and sarcosine against citalopram, and none for memantine, lanicemine, riluzole, D-cycloserine or the others.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Summary of main results › Efficacy: other glutamate receptor modulators; Results › 16.3, 19.1, 22.1

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract reports one odds ratio (3.94, 1.54 to 10.10; 185 participants, 7 studies) for an increase in 'response and remission' at 24 hours; in the summary-of-findings table and results 3.94 is the response estimate and remission is a separate estimate of 5.60 (1.07 to 29.46; 75 participants, 3 studies).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Main results, 4th paragraph; Summary of findings 1)
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the two outcomes separately from Summary of findings 1.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that against midazolam ketamine increases remission at 24 hours, with an interval of 0.67 to 7.32 (low certainty); the results describe the same estimate as uncertain because of wide confidence intervals.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Main results, 5th paragraph; Results › 2.3)
reporting_issues.consequence: No claim may say that ketamine increased remission compared with midazolam on this evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the esketamine dropout analysis as 4 studies; the summary-of-findings table and the results give 5 studies (773 participants, OR 1.58).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Main results, 6th paragraph; Summary of findings 3; Results › 9.9)

reporting_issues.issue: Certainty ranges in the text do not match the summary-of-findings tables: the Discussion gives very low to moderate for ketamine against placebo (Table 1: very low for every outcome) and against midazolam (Table 2: very low and low), and very low to high for esketamine (Table 3: low and moderate); the implications for research again give very low to high.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion › Quality of the evidence, 4th paragraph; Authors' conclusions › Implications for research; Summary of findings 1 to 3)
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the ratings in the summary-of-findings tables; no outcome reached high certainty.

reporting_issues.issue: The implications for practice say continued esketamine showed no effectiveness at 72 hours or one week (and the Discussion says no effect was found at those times); the results show significant score differences at 72 hours (SMD -0.30) and 1 week (-0.23) and a significant response difference at 1 week (OR 1.60); only response at 72 hours and remission at 72 hours and 1 week were not significant.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Authors' conclusions › Implications for practice, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Agreements and disagreements, 2nd paragraph; Results › 9.1, 9.3, 9.4)
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion misstates the esketamine time course; claims must use the per-outcome results.

reporting_issues.issue: The plain language summary says ketamine's effects lasted no more than one week and clearly disappeared after two weeks; the pooled depression-score difference against placebo at 4 weeks is significant (SMD -0.68, -1.07 to -0.29; 2 studies, 107), as is the single-study 4-week difference against midazolam (-0.57).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Plain language summary; Results › 1.4 and 2.4)
reporting_issues.consequence: The plain-language statement holds for response and remission, not for depression scores; the 4-week score estimate comes from trials that combined ketamine with a newly started antidepressant (see key findings).

reporting_issues.issue: In the midazolam comparison the text says sleepiness or drowsiness was more likely with ketamine but gives OR 0.21 (0.07 to 0.66), and the Discussion lists general malaise and sleepiness among the events more likely with ketamine although the results attribute general malaise to midazolam (OR 0.18).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › 2.2 Adverse events; Discussion › Summary of main results › Adverse events)
reporting_issues.consequence: Directions of these two adverse events cannot be taken from the text; the odds ratios below 1 indicate fewer events with ketamine.

reporting_issues.issue: Several single-study estimates are printed with I2 = 100% (for example sleepiness at 1 week against midazolam, ketamine against esketamine at 72 hours, ketamine against placebo at 3 months in Comparison 30), which is not possible for one study.

The text reports 174 excluded studies (44 for design, 26 secondary publications, 24 wrong population), but the excluded-studies table and the reference list give 18 studies, with reasons that do not reproduce those counts; one of them (Shiroma 2020, excluded for wrong design) is also an included study.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Excluded studies; Characteristics of excluded studies; References to studies excluded from this review)
reporting_issues.consequence: Exclusions cannot be audited; this drives AMSTAR 2 item 7.

reporting_issues.issue: The review allows studies in which fewer than 20% of participants have bipolar depression, but one included study does not meet that limit: the text gives Gálvez 2018 25% bipolar participants, and its characteristics table lists 1 bipolar participant among 5 (20%, editors' arithmetic); either figure is not below 20%. Loo 2012 (19.57%) sits just under the limit.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods › Types of participants › Comorbidities; Results › Included studies › Participants, 3rd paragraph; Characteristics of included studies › Gálvez 2018)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for the pooled estimates (Gálvez 2018 contributes only to the midazolam comparison at 4 weeks and 3 months), but the inclusion rule was not applied strictly.

reporting_issues.issue: Three prespecified sensitivity analyses (excluding trials with unclear allocation concealment or blinding, with unfair dose comparisons, and with imputed response rates or borrowed SDs) and the planned numbers needed to treat are not reported, and the differences-between-protocol-and-review section does not mention them.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods › Sensitivity analysis; Measures of treatment effect; Differences between protocol and review)
reporting_issues.consequence: The influence of the trials' unclear concealment and blinding on the pooled estimates is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The list of 14 studies at high risk of 'other bias' for industry funding omits Singh 2016 b, whose own risk-of-bias table rates other bias high for Janssen funding. Several 'low risk' allocation-concealment judgments are supported by quotations about randomization schedules or blinding rather than concealment (for example Chen 2017, Fedgchin 2019, Fu 2020, Ionescu 2020, Anderson 2017).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Other potential sources of bias; Characteristics of included studies › Singh 2016 b, Chen 2017, Fedgchin 2019, Fu 2020, Ionescu 2020, Anderson 2017)
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary counts of low-risk concealment and of industry-funded trials are not fully reliable.

reporting_issues.issue: The ketamine-placebo comparison pools trials in which ketamine was given with the anaesthetic at each ECT session (Anderson 2017, Chen 2017, Loo 2012) with standalone ketamine trials, and the esketamine comparison includes an ECT-anaesthesia trial (Jarventausta 2013) and an intravenous trial (Singh 2016 b) with the intranasal add-on trials; the only cognition result for ketamine against placebo comes from the ECT trial Chen 2017. Of the 16 placebo-controlled ketamine trials listed, two (Lapidus 2014, Shams Alizadeh 2015) contribute no data, without a reason given for Lapidus 2014.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Included studies › Interventions; 1. Ketamine versus placebo, 1st to 4th paragraphs; Characteristics of included studies › Anderson 2017, Chen 2017, Loo 2012, Jarventausta 2013, Lapidus 2014)
reporting_issues.consequence: Pooled estimates beyond 72 hours mix different questions (ketamine with ECT against ECT alone, and ketamine alone against placebo); claims about ketamine as an antidepressant on its own should use the sensitivity analysis without the ECT trials.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion infers from no difference in suicidal ideation in two small trials that ketamine is not an effective treatment for suicidality, and from the esketamine results that esketamine is not effective in reducing suicidal ideation; the implications add that neither drug prevents relapse at three months, which no included trial tested.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion › Summary of main results › Efficacy: Ketamine versus placebo, 1st paragraph; Efficacy: esketamine, 3rd paragraph; Authors' conclusions › Implications for research, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of a significant difference in small samples is not evidence of no effect; these statements should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: No declarations of interest are printed for two of the twelve listed authors (Annabelle Barnes, Rebecca Smith). Minor data-entry errors appear elsewhere: a propofol dose given as 99.5 mg/kg (Jarventausta 2013) and a ketamine dose of 40.2 mg/kg (Loo 2012) are implausible units; a memantine remission odds ratio is printed as -0.11 with the interval of the corresponding SMD; Correia-Melo 2020 is given a baseline MADRS mean of 3.1 in the esketamine arm against 32.9 in the ketamine arm.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Declarations of interest; Characteristics of included studies › Jarventausta 2013, Loo 2012, Correia-Melo 2020; Results › 10.3)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; numbers taken from the characteristics tables should be checked against the primary trials.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8434915 (version with the amendments of 13 September and 17 November 2021): abstract, plain language summary, background, objectives and methods in full; all three summary-of-findings tables; results in full, including the subgroup and sensitivity analyses and the other glutamate receptor modulators; discussion and authors' conclusions; what's new and history; acknowledgements; differences between protocol and review; contributions of authors; sources of support; declarations of interest; the Data and analyses summary tables (Comparisons 1, 2, 9 and 23 to 35); the characteristics of included studies for every ketamine and esketamine trial with data (Anderson 2017, Arabzadeh 2018, Berman 2000, Canuso 2018, Chen 2017, Chen 2018, Correia-Melo 2020, Daly 2018, Fava 2018, Fedgchin 2019, Fu 2020, Gálvez 2018, Ghasemi 2013, Grunebaum 2018, Hu 2016, Ionescu 2018, Ionescu 2020, Jarventausta 2013, Lapidus 2014, Li 2016, Loo 2012, Murrough 2013, Ochs-Ross 2020, Popova 2019, Shiroma 2020, Singh 2016 a, Singh 2016 b, Sos 2013, Su 2017, Sumner 2020, Tiger 2020, Zarate 2006a) and the characteristics of excluded studies; search-strategy appendices skimmed (the review has no separate online supplement; its appendices are part of the page). Forest plots, the study flow diagram and the risk-of-bias figures are images and were not read. No correction or erratum is linked from the page.
